did_you_know.text: Did you know? In this chapter, Jerusalem is described as a “strong city,” whose walls and ramparts are fortified not with stone but with the salvation the Lord provides.
Did you know? The city gates are commanded to open so that a “righteous nation” may enter—a people described as faithful.
Did you know? The repeated phrase “perfect peace” emphasizes the peace the Lord grants to those who trust in him and remain inwardly steadfast.
Did you know? Isaiah calls the Lord the “Rock eternal” and presents trust in him as a firm and everlasting foundation.
Did you know? The chapter contrasts the exalted city, which the Lord brings down to the dust, with the city protected by salvation.
Did you know? After the exalted city is humbled, it is the feet of the poor and needy that are described as trampling it.
Did you know? The soul’s longing for the Lord is described both at night and through the spirit within a person; God’s judgment teaches the inhabitants of the world righteousness.

Did you know? According to the chapter, even if the wicked are shown grace, they do not learn righteousness; in the land of uprightness they continue to do wrong and do not recognize the Lord’s majesty.
Did you know? This verse expresses explicit hope for resurrection: the Lord’s dead will live, and the bodies of the departed will rise, awake, and sing for joy.
Did you know? Before the wrath passes, the Lord commands his people to hide in their rooms and shut the doors for a short time.
